A1.en_short: Talking about yourself: who you are or how you feel now.
Saying what you are not, or where you are not.
Asking about someone's name, job or how they feel.
Talking about one person (he or she): who they are or how they feel.
Talking about yourself and other people: who we are or how we are.
Talking about other people (they): who they are or how they feel.
Words that show who owns something: my, our, your, her, their.
A1.example: Our house is near your school.

A1.en_short: Words used after a verb or preposition: me, us, him, her, them.
Pointing at things near or far: this is, that is.
Talking about things, places or times: it is.
Using a or an before a singular, countable noun: a book, an apple.
A1.example: I have a dog and an umbrella.

A1.en_short: Using the for a specific thing that both people know about.
Using some and any with plural or uncountable nouns.
A1.example: Do you have any money? I have some.

A1.en_short: Saying there is not any of something.
Words that connect a noun to other words: in, on, at, to, for.
A1.example: The cat is under the table.

A1.en_short: Words for people or things that are not specific: nobody, anything.
Words that show how often something happens: always, often, sometimes.
Words that make an adjective or adverb stronger: really, so, very.
Showing that something never happens.
Comparing two things by adding -er to a short adjective.
A1.example: My brother is taller than me.

A1.en_short: Saying something is the biggest or best with -est.
A1.example: She is the tallest girl in class.

A1.en_short: Phrasal verbs: a verb plus a particle, such as 'get up' or 'turn on'.
Phrasal verbs with a verb, a particle and a preposition, such as 'look forward to'.
A1.example: I look forward to the trip.

A1.en_short: The verb be in positive sentences: I am, you are, he is.
The verb be in negative sentences: I am not, we are not.
Questions with the verb be: Are you...? Is she...?
Positive sentences with simple present verbs: I work, we live.
Negative sentences with simple present verbs: I do not work.
Questions with simple present verbs: Do you work? Does she like?
Positive sentences with he, she or it: she works, it costs.
Actions happening now: I am reading, they are playing.
Positive sentences with was or were: I was, they were.
Positive sentences with simple past verbs: I walked, she visited.
Passive sentences for the present: The room is cleaned every day.
The infinitive with to: to do, to go.
A verb followed by to and an infinitive: I want to go.
A verb with an object and to plus an infinitive: I want you to help.
The -ing form used as a noun: Swimming is fun.
A preposition followed by an -ing form: before leaving, after eating.
Verbs followed by an -ing form: I enjoy reading.
Positive commands: Sit down. Open the door.
Let's plus a verb to suggest doing something: Let's go.
Positive sentences with can, to say you are able to do something.
Questions with can: Can you swim?
There is and there are, to say that something exists.
A1.example: There is a cat on the roof.

A1.en_short: Joining words like and, but and or to link ideas.
A1.example: I like tea but she likes coffee.

A1.en_short: Using when to talk about the time of an action: when I arrive.
Connecting words that add extra ideas: because, before, although, while.
A1.example: I stayed home because I was sick.

A1.en_short: Verbs like hope, know and think followed by a clause, without that.
A present participle after a noun: the boy running.
A1.example: The man standing there is my uncle.

A1.en_short: A past participle before a noun: the broken window.
A past participle after a noun: the book written by...
A1.example: The book written by him is famous.

A1.en_short: Relative pronoun 'who' for people as the subject: the man who lives here.
A1.example: The woman who lives next door is a nurse.

A1.en_short: Relative pronoun 'that' as the subject: the book that is on the table.
A1.example: The girl that called you is my friend.

A1.en_short: Relative pronoun left out when it is the object: the book I read.
A1.example: The movie we watched was funny.

A1.en_short: A preposition at the end of a sentence: Who are you talking to?
The basic sentence pattern: subject + verb + object.
Questions with the basic pattern: Do you like pizza?
Questions with 'Why': Why are you late?
Questions with 'What': What is this?
Questions with 'Where': Where do you live?
Questions with 'How': How are you?
Questions with 'How' and an adjective or adverb: How old is he? How often?

A2.en_short: This and that before a noun: this book, that car.
Another for one more: another cup of tea.
Much with uncountable nouns: much time, much money.
Ones replaces a plural noun: the red ones.
Comparing with more and an adjective or adverb: more interesting.
Saying the most with most and an adjective or adverb: the most expensive.
A2.example: It is the most expensive hotel.

A2.en_short: Phrasal verbs with an object in the middle or at the end: turn it off.
The present perfect in positive sentences: I have finished.
Negative sentences with was or were: I was not at home.
Negative sentences with simple past verbs: I did not go.
Questions with simple past verbs: Did you see it?
Actions in progress in the past: I was sleeping.
A2.example: I was cooking when you called.

A2.en_short: Future with will in positive sentences: I will call you.
Passive sentences for the past: The letter was sent.
A verb followed by an object and an -ing form: I saw him running.
A2.example: I saw him crossing the street.

A2.en_short: Talking about plans and future intentions: I am going to travel.
A2.example: I am going to study tonight.

A2.en_short: Positive sentences with have to, for something necessary: I have to work.
Positive sentences with need to, for something you must do: I need to go.
Positive sentences with should, for advice: You should rest.
Positive sentences with will, for predictions and decisions.
Positive sentences with would, for polite requests and imagined situations.
Verbs followed by a clause with that: I think that you are right.
A2.example: He said that he was tired.

A2.en_short: Clauses with if for real or possible conditions: If it rains, we stay home.
A2.example: If it rains, we will stay.

A2.en_short: Clauses with as, meaning while or because.
A2.example: As I was leaving, it started to rain.

A2.en_short: A present participle before a noun: the sleeping cat.
The compound relative 'what', meaning the thing that: What I need is time.
Relative adverbs for places, times and reasons: where, when, why.
A2.example: This is the place where we met.

A2.en_short: Negative sentences with the basic pattern: I do not like it.
Reporting what someone said: He said that..., She explained...
Indirect questions with know, wonder or understand: Do you know where it is?
Verbs like have, let and make followed by an object and a base verb.
Polite questions with can: Can you help me?

B1.en_short: You are and you are not, with the verb be.
These and those before a noun: these shoes, those houses.
Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, ours, theirs.
Reflexive pronouns: myself, yourself, himself, themselves.
Each other, used when two or more people do the same thing to one another.
Others, used for other people or things.
B1.example: Some like tea; others like coffee.

B1.en_short: Adjectives after words ending in -thing: something new, nothing important.
Adverbs showing the speaker's attitude: fortunately, unfortunately.
Stronger comparatives with a lot, far, even or still: much better, far better.
Negative sentences with he, she or it: she does not work.
Negative sentences with actions in progress: I am not working.
Negative sentences with the present perfect: I have not finished.
The past perfect in positive sentences: I had finished.
B1.example: She had left before I arrived.

B1.en_short: Negative sentences with will: I will not go.
Passive sentences with modal verbs: It can be done.
Get plus a past participle, often for changes or things happening: get married.
B1.example: He got hurt in the game.

B1.en_short: The negative infinitive: not to do, not to go.
B1.example: He told me not to wait.

B1.en: To-infinitive with its own subject: for + noun + to do
B1.en_short: An infinitive with its own subject: for him to decide.
B1.example: It is easy for children to learn.

B1.en_short: Be + to + infinitive for official plans or instructions: You are to wait here.
B1.example: We are to meet at six.

B1.en_short: Negative commands: Do not touch that.
Saying you have the skill or ability to do something: I am able to swim.
Could, for ability in the past or polite requests: I could swim.
B1.example: I could run fast when I was young.

B1.en_short: Negative sentences with could: I could not swim.
May, for possibility or permission: It may rain.
Might, for a possible but uncertain result: It might rain.
Must, for strong obligation or deduction: You must wear a seatbelt.
B1.example: You must wear a seat belt.

B1.en_short: Negative sentences with need to: I do not need to go.
Negative sentences with should: You should not do that.
Used to, for past habits or situations no longer true: I used to play.
Negative sentences with will: I will not forget.
Here is and here are, to point at something: Here is the bus.
Asking about information with a clause that starts with a wh- word: I know where he is.
Wh- words followed by to and an infinitive: I don't know what to do.
B1.example: I don't know what to do.

B1.en_short: Clauses that add extra information, set off by commas: My brother, who lives in Paris, ...
B1.example: My brother, who lives in Lima, is a doctor.

B1.en_short: Adverbs that start a clause without a noun before them: where, when, why.
The basic sentence pattern with a verb and no object: The sun rises.
Reporting what someone told you: She told me that...
B1.example: He told me he was leaving.

B1.en_short: Indirect questions with ask, remind, show, teach or tell: Ask him where he lives.
B1.example: She asked me what time it was.

B1.en_short: Ask or tell plus an object and to plus an infinitive: I asked him to come.
Participle clauses, such as 'Walking home, I saw...'
B1.example: Walking home, I met a friend.

B1.en_short: The second conditional for imagined or unlikely situations: If I had money, I would travel.
B1.example: If I had money, I would travel.

B2.en_short: It is not, or it is not there.
B2.example: It is not far from here.

B2.en_short: Pronoun meaning none of something: None of them came.
B2.example: None of them came.

B2.en_short: Saying two things are equal with as ... as: as big as.
B2.example: He is as tall as his father.

B2.en_short: Comparing with less and least, to say something is smaller in amount or degree.
B2.example: This route is less crowded.

B2.en_short: Enough after an adjective or adverb: good enough, quickly enough.
B2.example: He is old enough to drive.

B2.en_short: Such before an adjective and noun: such a nice day.
B2.example: It was such a long day.

B2.en_short: Emphatic do and does, to stress a verb: I do like it.
B2.example: I do like your idea.

B2.en_short: Actions that started in the past and are still going on: I have been working.
B2.example: I have been studying all day.

B2.en_short: Other ways to talk about the future: will be doing, going to, about to.
B2.example: This time tomorrow I will be flying.

B2.en_short: Passive present negative sentences: The door is not locked.
B2.example: The shop is not opened on Sundays.

B2.en_short: Passive present perfect sentences: The work has been finished.
B2.example: The window has been broken.

B2.en_short: Passive future sentences: It will be sent tomorrow.
B2.example: The work will be finished soon.

B2.en: Indirect object as subject of passive
B2.en_short: Making the indirect object the subject of a passive: He was given a prize.
B2.example: She was given a present.

B2.en_short: The passive infinitive: to be done, to be seen.
B2.example: She wants to be invited.

B2.en_short: In order to plus an infinitive, to show purpose: in order to pass.
B2.example: I study in order to pass.

B2.en_short: Not followed by an -ing form: not knowing what to say.
B2.example: Not knowing the answer is normal.

B2.en_short: Being plus a past participle, for passive states: being watched.
B2.example: I hate being told what to do.

B2.en_short: Negative have to, to say something is not necessary: I do not have to go.
B2.example: You don't have to come.

B2.en_short: Negative might: It might not work.
B2.example: She might not come.

B2.en_short: Negative would: I would not do that.
B2.example: She wouldn't say why.

B2.en_short: Modal plus a continuous form, for guesses about now: He must be working.
B2.example: He must be sleeping.

B2.en_short: Modal plus a perfect form, for past guesses: She might have forgotten.
B2.example: She must have left.

B2.en_short: Negative modal plus a perfect form: He could not have known.
B2.example: He can't have seen us.

B2.en_short: Whether, meaning if, in indirect questions: I wonder whether it is true.
B2.example: I don't know whether he will come.

B2.en_short: So that, to show purpose: I left early so that I could catch the train.
B2.example: I spoke slowly so that he could understand.

B2.en_short: The relative pronoun 'which' as the subject: the car, which is old.
B2.example: The bus which goes downtown is late.

B2.en_short: The relative pronoun 'who' as the object: the man who I met.
B2.example: The man who I met was nice.

B2.en_short: The relative pronoun 'whom' as the object, in formal English: the man whom I met.
B2.example: The person whom I called was away.

B2.en_short: The relative pronoun 'which' as the object: the book which I read.
B2.example: The book which I read was long.

B2.en_short: The relative pronoun 'that' as the object: the book that I read.
B2.example: The film that we saw was great.

B2.en_short: A preposition before a relative pronoun: the house in which I was born.
B2.example: The house in which I was born is old.

B2.en_short: Words with -ever, meaning any: whoever, whatever, wherever.
B2.example: Whoever calls, tell them I'm out.

B2.en_short: Have or get plus an object and a past participle: I had my car repaired.
B2.example: I had my hair cut.

B2.en_short: Asking who did something: Who called you?
B2.example: Who is that man?
